column2: Act Two
Golden Eyes
It was the painting’s oppressive power.

In it, the sky was iron-gray mingled with the color of flames. A single enormous tree stood beneath it, its dead branches reaching in every direction, weaving a dense web that held up the cracked heavens.
Bones littered the wasteland. A black beast was rising from deep within the heaps of remains, skulls hanging from its wings. It spread those vast membranes and breathed black fire into the sky.
A piercing roar echoed inside Lu Mingfei’s head. Incredibly, he felt he could hear the creature screaming.
Amid the bustling crowd, Lu Mingfei glanced at the ticket in his hand, then up at the cathedral-like dome of Chicago’s railway station.

A huge suitcase stood on either side of him; together they weighed almost as much as he did. His backpack bulged where his aunt had stuffed in a pressure cooker. A woven plastic sack held a twelve-hole hollow-fiber quilt, his pillow was strapped to a suitcase, and his passport was clenched between his teeth.

Heaven’s chosen son and newly minted international student Lu Mingfei had brought his entire overseas survival kit across the ocean on a United Airlines flight, landing alone at Chicago’s international airport. According to the itinerary Norma had prepared, he would take the CC1000 Express from the station to Cassell College.
“I really wish I could take you myself, but I have to fly to Russia,” Professor Guderian had said regretfully over the phone. “Don’t worry, though. Norma will arrange everything.”

Norma was indeed an outstanding secretary. Three weeks later, a gigantic envelope reached him containing everything from his passport to his itinerary, plus Cassell College Enrollment for Dummies, labeled underneath: Lu Mingfei Edition.
Despite its ridiculous title, the guide proved extremely useful—until he reached Chicago’s railway station.

“The CC1000 Express? Never heard of it… Perhaps a branch-line train? But that number doesn’t sound right… The new timetable lists every service. Check again… The ticket looks genuine, but I really don’t know any such train.” Different station employees all gave him versions of the same answer.
There was no such express in the timetable.
“This is one hell of a screwup!” Lu Mingfei wanted to tear his hair out in the middle of the crowd.

God promised Moses, Go to Canaan, the land of milk and honey, and gave him a map. With divine power, Moses crossed the vast Red Sea, escaped his Egyptian pursuers, and barely survived—only to find signposts reading TO INDIA, TO CHINA, and TO JAPAN, with no TO CANAAN anywhere. The friendly policeman below the signs said, “Canaan? No idea. Never heard of it!”
That was approximately how Lu Mingfei felt.

He had only twenty dollars left. His aunt had given him five hundred for traveling expenses. But at Chicago customs, a chubby officer had counted the dozens of pirated PS2 discs he had brought, written a terrifying figure on a receipt, and complimented his taste all at once. “Oh? Resident Evil 4! Ha! You like Dynasty Warriors, too? Hey! I love Dragon Quest!…”
Perhaps out of appreciation for his taste, the fat officer had left him twenty dollars.

Now this Moses from across the world stood outside Subway, clutching his single twenty-dollar bill, wondering whether to grit his teeth and go hungry or buy a sandwich-and-Coke combo. Whatever the merits of that thirty-six-thousand-dollar scholarship, he had only twenty dollars now. Spend six and fourteen remained. How many more days could he last? Perhaps he should save his food money to buy a phone card and call the college. He had no phone. His uncle had kept that N96 as a treasured farewell gift.
“One dollar, just one dollar…” someone said behind him.
It was the standard American beggar’s refrain, much like the rhythmic songs of beggars in old China.
“No! I am poor! No money!” Lu Mingfei replied in plain, economical English.

He turned to inspect the tall, burly young man behind him. The face buried in a full beard was rather handsome, his candle-bright eyes full of yearning. His dark-green plaid shirt and loose, dragging trousers looked as though they hadn’t been changed or washed in ages. A beggar like this was a rare sight in America. The others dressed better.
“Chinese?” Recognizing his nationality, the man instantly switched to fluent Chinese. “Kind sir, spare enough for a Coke. I’m really not a beggar. I just lost my wallet while traveling.”
You know the begging patter in both Chinese and English that well, and you’re claiming you’re not a professional? Lu Mingfei thought.
“Fingel von Frings. Really not a beggar. A college student.” To prove it, the young man took a dictionary-sized textbook from the shoulder bag behind him.
Its title was in a mixture of English and Latin. The book looked old, and Lu Mingfei seemed to have seen that sort of writing somewhere before.
This guy actually spoke fluent Chinese… A thought flashed through his mind. He had seen that style of writing on his Cassell College admission documents.
“Are you waiting for… the CC1000 Express?” he asked.
Each took a magnetic ticket from his pocket. They were identical: black cards bearing a silver image of a vast, leafy tree.
“I’m a freshman. Lu Mingfei.” He offered his hand in friendship.
“One of my own! At last, someone who can give me a dollar for a Coke.” Fingel seized his hand.
Is there anything besides Coke inside that bird’s nest you call a head? Lu Mingfei thought.
“Brother, I admire you. You look like a loyal friend!” Sprawled across a bench, Fingel took great bites of a sandwich and drank Lu Mingfei’s Coke.

Between them, they had twenty-five dollars. Since Coke came with free refills, Lu Mingfei suggested they needn’t buy two cups. All they needed were two straws and twice as many refills. Fingel came from Germany, an advanced capitalist nation, but showed none of the supposed German fastidiousness about hygiene. He enthusiastically praised his Chinese schoolmate’s ingenuity.
“What year are you in, senior?” Lu Mingfei asked.
“Eighth.”
“Eighth?” Lu Mingfei choked on his Coke.
“Well, fourth, actually. I repeated a year,” Fingel said.
“Then how is it eighth?”
“Repeated it four years running…”
Deeply concerned about his future, Lu Mingfei decided to avoid the terrifying subject of repeating years. “Have you taken that train before?”

“Every semester. Otherwise you have to take a helicopter. The campus is in the mountains. This is the only train that goes there. Nobody knows its timetable—nobody at Chicago station, anyway. The last conductor who knew its schedule died two years ago. He said it had been running since before World War II,” Fingel said. “Don’t worry. A train always comes eventually. Low-ranking people just have to wait.”
“Ranking? What’s that? The bourgeoisie and the proletariat?” Lu Mingfei asked.
“Something like aristocratic status. Higher-ranked students get privileges. College resources go to them first. Like having a train sent for you sooner.”
“Eight years here, and your rank still isn’t high enough?”
“To tell the truth, I’m caught between being expelled and scrambling for enough credits!” Fingel spread his hands.
“Is it easy to find work after graduating from Cassell? You’ve spent four years in your fourth year and still don’t want to drop out?”
“No. They assign you a job!” Fingel belched loudly.

Lu Mingfei looked through the station’s floor-to-ceiling windows. Dark skyscrapers stood shoulder to shoulder like giants. Night had fallen over Chicago. Trains scattered bright sparks as they passed along the elevated tracks. Pedestrians hurried by; neon lights flashed.

He and Fingel had spent two nights at the station. Without hotel money, they could only wrap themselves in blankets and sleep on the waiting-room benches. Had their magnetic tickets not actually worked in the gates, security would have thrown them out long ago. Yet no one at the station knew anything about the mysterious CC1000 branch-line express.

Fingel didn’t care. Every trip back to college was like this, he said. They could only blame their low rank. High-ranking students were met by a train on arrival and boarded through a VIP entrance without causing a stir. Lu Mingfei had to ask just how low their ranks were. Roughly medieval serf level, Fingel said. Seeing his spirits fall, he added consolingly that there were ranks below serfs. Some people ranked about level with mules.

Only the two of them remained in the waiting hall. Fingel wandered about with his textbook, his reading echoing through the huge space. Lu Mingfei wrapped himself in his blanket and curled up on a wooden bench. As his mind grew hazy, he dimly heard distant bells.

The bells echoed, apparently from a faraway church. Eyes closed, his thoughts wandered: a wasteland under the moon; a dark church silhouette in the distance; crowds running across the wilderness with torches that couldn’t light their faces, leaving them hidden in shadow. They ran toward a full moon, impossibly large, half sunk below the horizon. From a mountaintop, those people leaped toward it.
He started. Why had he thought of that? Mad, magnificent, and real—as though he had witnessed that splendid scene himself.

Why were those bells so monotonous? Something was wrong. He was in Chicago. Outside lay busy roads, noise, a hubbub of voices. Why could he hear only that solitary, monotonous tolling? There shouldn’t have been a church nearby.

He sat up. An enormous moon was slowly rising beyond the windows. Moonlight flooded in like a tide approaching the shore. The whole waiting hall lay beneath its cool, watery light. Window frames cast shadows across the bench backs. A boy sat in silence, his face lifted toward the moon.

Lu Mingfei looked around. Fingel was gone. So were the guards at the entrance. The distant Subway had switched off its lights. Only he and the boy remained. It was strange, but he dared not speak or even breathe hard. The silence filling the hall felt impossible to break.

The boy looked Chinese, about thirteen or fourteen, in a jet-black little evening suit. Light flowed over his young face. Lu Mingfei couldn’t understand why a child that age wore a silence and sorrow that said, I have lived for thousands of years. Nor why, with so many empty benches, he had chosen to sit beside him, as though waiting for him to wake.
Lu Mingfei lifted off the blanket and sat beside the boy. They watched the moonlight without a word. Time flowed slowly, as if they were two people watching the sea.
“Shall we trade?” the boy asked softly.
“What? What?” Lu Mingfei didn’t understand.
“Shall we trade?” the boy asked again.
“Trade what? I don’t have money… I am poor, no money…”
“So you’re still refusing?” The boy slowly turned his head. Flame-like light flowed through his golden pupils, like a mirror reflecting fire.
In an instant, that fire swallowed Lu Mingfei’s entire consciousness. His body convulsed. As though facing mortal danger, a tremendous force erupted inside him. He jerked backward.
“Ah!” Fingel’s scream jolted him awake.

Fingel was crouched nearby, clutching his head. Noise came from outside: footsteps, car horns, wheels grinding against rails, every sound of the metropolis. Two guards dozed against the doorway. The distant Subway was still lit.
Another dream? Lu Mingfei thought.

He had never had two dreams stacked together before. In the first, crowds ran across a wasteland. In the second, he spoke to a boy. He had woken from the first straight into the second, when he had really been asleep on the bench all along, without even lifting his blanket.
“Don’t do the high jump in your sleep! You just leaped like a startled flea!” Fingel complained.
Lu Mingfei wiped sweat from his forehead. Why had he been frightened? The boy’s golden eyes? What was strange about golden eyes? The anime-club girls wore colored contacts in every shade imaginable.
“Get your luggage. The train’s here,” Fingel said.

He heard bells and a train whistle. Fingel was right. A train had just arrived, its headlights sweeping the platform. At two in the morning, on a night with no extra services scheduled, the CC1000 Express pulled in.

A dark figure appeared beside the empty ticket gate: a man in an old-fashioned dark-green conductor’s uniform, with a gold badge on his cap. He rang a little gold bell and carried a flashlight and a card reader.
“CC1000 Express. Passengers, please prepare to board. Passengers, please prepare to board.” His voice echoed through the hall.

The guards went on sleeping. Only Fingel seemed to notice the conductor. No one even looked out from the brightly lit Subway. A man in such an antiquated uniform appearing in a modern Chicago station in the middle of the night ought to have been remarkable. Yet nobody noticed him.
Lu Mingfei shivered. The conductor was like a… ghost!
“Why does it feel like… a train to hell?” He grabbed Fingel’s sleeve.
“Just the effect of his Yanling. Perfectly ordinary living guy. A Backstreet Boys fan, too,” Fingel said.
“Yanling?” Lu Mingfei stared.
“We’re here! Fingel and Lu Mingfei!” Fingel waved.

Lu Mingfei cautiously took out his ticket and followed him toward the gate, dragging his bags. Only when he saw the conductor’s face did he believe Fingel. The man really didn’t look like a ghost. He was chewing gum and blowing bubbles.
The conductor swiped Fingel’s ticket. A green light came on with a beep.
“Still haven’t dropped out, Fingel? I thought I wouldn’t see you this year.”
“I finish what I start,” Fingel said. “Train’s awfully late. Did my rank drop again?”
“To F. You started at A, remember. You’ve fallen all the way from heaven to hell.”
“Really gone from serf to livestock…” Fingel muttered.
Lu Mingfei’s ticket passed through the reader. The light turned green, but this time cheerful music played.

“Lu Mingfei?” The conductor’s beautiful green eyes brightened. “Terribly sorry. A dispatching error. You’re S-rank, but we get so few people that high that the system must have malfunctioned. Like the millennium bug.”
“S?” Fingel’s eyes widened. “Isn’t the principal the only S?”
“Not the only one. But there are no more than ten,” the conductor said. “Hurry aboard. We don’t stop long.”

“Can I ask something… Is this really an official train? Why isn’t it in the timetable? Why didn’t it arrive on time?” He couldn’t help himself. Everything about it was uncanny. If it really was the Hell Express, at least he could say a prayer before boarding.

“Of course. Specially approved by Chicago’s city government, direct to Cassell College. It isn’t listed because it’s an irregular branch-line service. You know those special trains that use the public railway but go to particular mines or factories? We’re like those.” The conductor answered straightforwardly, without a hint of mystery.

They followed him onto the platform. The high-speed train waited on the tracks, headlights dazzling. It was black and streamlined, with brilliant silver-white vines spreading over the paintwork, magnificent as a work of art. Outside its one open sliding door stood a familiar figure: Professor Guderian.

The train raced through the black night. Across a narrow oak table, Lu Mingfei and Fingel faced Professor Guderian. The carriage was elegantly European, its walls covered in Victorian-patterned wallpaper, its windows framed in solid wood. Dark-green leather sofas were embroidered with gold. Every detail was exquisite. Both boys had changed into Cassell uniforms: white shirts, dark-green suits edged in silver, deep rose-red neck scarves, the college’s World Tree emblem embroidered on their breast pockets. No college tailor had ever measured Lu Mingfei, yet the clothes fit perfectly. Turning back a cuff, he found a name stitched inside in dark-green thread: Ricardo M. Lu.
The moment he boarded this train and put on these clothes, he felt he had become upper class. Extremely upper class.
Yet he couldn’t help feeling afraid, for no clear reason, as though something terrible were about to happen.
“Coffee or hot chocolate?” Professor Guderian asked. He sat against the wall, a huge canvas-covered painting behind him.
“Hot chocolate.” Fingel raised his hand.
“I wasn’t asking you. Be serious. I’m your temporary adviser, assigned by the college. This is freshman orientation.” The professor looked at Lu Mingfei. “You could have something stronger, too.”
“You can… drink alcohol while meeting your adviser?”
“They just give you something to calm your nerves so you don’t start screaming halfway through orientation,” Fingel whispered.
“Is… is it that bad?” Lu Mingfei shrank back.

“Worse… than you think,” the professor said quietly. “First, I’m sorry I’m late. Russia held me up longer than expected. Only after returning did I discover the dispatching error and that you still hadn’t been collected, so I came along on the train. Second, every student must take an entrance qualification exam. We call it the 3E exam. Without passing, you cannot be admitted, and your scholarship cannot take effect yet.”
“A qualification exam?” Lu Mingfei relaxed. “Still frightening… but at least my heart survived that.”
“Please sign this confidentiality agreement.” The professor handed him a document.

His hand trembled over the strange mixture of Latin and English, but he signed. The train was carrying him toward mysterious Cassell College at more than two hundred kilometers an hour. This was the road his parents had pointed out. What could he refuse now?

Professor Guderian carefully put it away. “As a legitimate university registered with the U.S. Department of Education, Cassell College has always offered high-quality education to students of exceptional talent, along with help finding jobs. Our normal course lasts four years. People like Fingel, who haven’t graduated after eight, are very rare. We follow a traditional residential system. All students must live on campus. At graduation, you receive an official degree. Unfortunately, our degrees may not correspond to subjects available at other universities. If you wish to pursue a master’s or doctorate, you will have to remain here.”
“You mean… it isn’t a proper degree?” Lu Mingfei grew wary.
“No, quite proper. Our degrees fully meet the department’s requirements. I mean that our subject is unusual.” The professor chose his words. “Extremely unusual.”
“How… unusual?” Lu Mingfei blinked.
“You know what a seminary is?”
He nodded.

“A seminary is a specialized school whose students mainly study God. Medical schools principally study the workings of the human body. Business schools examine the ancient question of exchange. Cassell is another such specialized institution. What we study is…”
He stood, seized a corner of the canvas covering the enormous oil painting behind him, and whipped it away.
The terrible scene lay exposed beneath the lights. The instant Lu Mingfei looked at it, he felt as though an enormous force would fling him backward.
It was the painting’s oppressive power.

In it, the sky was iron-gray mingled with the color of flames. A single enormous tree stood beneath it, its dead branches reaching in every direction, weaving a dense web that held up the cracked heavens. Bones littered the wasteland. A black beast rose from deep within the heaps of remains, skulls hanging from its wings. It spread those vast membranes and breathed black fire into the sky.
A piercing roar echoed inside Lu Mingfei’s head. Incredibly, he felt he could hear the creature screaming.
“A dragon?” His voice trembled.

“Yes. A dragon. More precisely, the Dragon Emperor Nidhogg. According to the Poetic Edda of Norse mythology, at Ragnarök it will gnaw through the roots of Yggdrasil, the World Tree. On that day, the world will end.” Professor Guderian ran his fingers over the neatly shelved, finely bound ancient books. “If you knew Latin, you could read their titles. Dragon Genealogy, Dragons and Yanling, The Key of Solomon, On Dragon Bloodlines, Dragon Genetics… Thousands of years of accumulated knowledge. Countless generations have sought and studied dragons. Cassell brings it all together. Here you can study alchemical engineering, magic-powered mechanical design, theories of dragon lineage, and other disciplines. Every course has the same ultimate goal.” He looked directly into Lu Mingfei’s eyes. “Slaying dragons!”
“S-slaying dragons?”

“Slaying dragons.” The professor nodded. “In places you know nothing of, this has gone on for thousands of years. Humanity has written one history without dragons, but another history bears their presence on every line. The secret is too astonishing. If it escaped, the consequences would be impossible to predict. So for thousands of years, certain families we call the Bloodline Clans have held it together and shouldered the duty of killing dragons. They trained descendants in combat, incantations, magic, and alchemy, sending them onto the battlefield to bury one attempt at a dragon revival after another. Today, Cassell College carries on their legacy.”
“Their… legacy?”

“Yes. The old dragon-slaying families were vast, and most have died out. In this new era, we can no longer rely on family succession. We need a modern educational system.” He offered his hand. “Welcome to Cassell College, Lu Mingfei!”

“Could you… not stick out your hand and welcome me before I’ve decided? Your college is a vocational school for dragon slayers? Please!” Lu Mingfei’s face twitched. “Can we keep the joke within reason? What is this, the opening cinematic of a new Dragon Quest? How did I get inside your cinematic? Could someone give me a portal out?”
A world-shattering crash. The entire train rocked. Every light flickered and died. Darkness fell.
“Hey! Did we hit a mountain?” He felt himself over. Apparently unhurt. “Anyone injured? Anyone know where the candles are?”
“Lu Mingfei, everything they said is true,” someone said softly in the dark.
The lights returned. The same luxurious train, the same leather sofa. But Professor Guderian and Fingel were gone. He turned. The boy from his dream at Chicago station sat beside him.
“Y-you… where did you get on?” he stammered.
“I’ve been here all along. I was waiting for the train, just like you,” the boy said mildly.
“You sound like a vengeful ghost…”
“Look outside,” the boy said. “Welcome… to the realm of dragons!”
Following his gaze, Lu Mingfei looked out the window. His pupils dilated. Before that world, he lost even the strength to breathe.

It was no longer dark. The train sped across an immense ice field. White ice with a faint blue sheen covered a mountain stabbing into the sky. The heavens were blood-red. Torrential rain fell, every drop crimson, running down the windows. Atop the ice peak lay the dragon from the painting, motionless, its wings reaching all the way to the foot of the mountain. Thick, reeking blood stained the entire peak. Crowds climbed its wings. Those who reached the summit gathered around its head and drove sharp iron spikes into its skull, hammering fiercely at their ends. Each time they bored a hole, white fluid spouted like a fountain, then quickly evaporated into dense white vapor. They cheered and leaped, their cries shaking the sky.

“Nidhogg, the Black Dragon King. Thousands of years ago, he was killed on his own throne. His throne was that mountain, eternally covered in ice and snow. His killers left his enormous corpse on its summit, wings hanging to its foot. Blood ran down like lava, staining the mountain red and melting the ice. Blood-colored vapor rose into the sky, became dark-red clouds, and fell as scarlet rain. His killers bathed in it and cheered. They called that day the beginning of the New Era,” the boy said softly.
“Oh… God!” Lu Mingfei trembled at the distant sound of hammers striking iron spikes.
“This is the oldest emperor, unrecorded in history. On the day he died, everyone rejoiced.” The boy’s voice was calm.
He seemed to enjoy the hammering enormously, closing his eyes to savor it in silence, a faint smile on his face.
“How wonderful. Without that day, the world would never have become what it is.” He opened his eyes and looked at Lu Mingfei.
Somehow, Lu Mingfei felt such terrible sadness in his smile.
Thousands of years… of sadness.
“You and that black dragon…” he ventured. “Were you close?”
“No. Not at all. Quite the opposite,” the boy whispered. “I am the one who most wants to kill him. No one in this world wants him dead more than I do!”
Lu Mingfei opened his eyes to find himself lying on a leather couch beneath a blanket. He was in an elegantly old-fashioned study, bookcases all around and a crystal chandelier overhead.
He sat up and looked around. Professor Guderian was dozing at a nearby desk.
“You’re awake?” The professor raised his disheveled head.
“Where are we? Did the train overturn? I just heard this huge crash.” He pressed his forehead. A blood vessel seemed to throb inside his skull.

“We’re at Cassell. The journey was perfectly smooth. Why would we hit a mountain? You were so frightened during orientation that you fainted. We had to carry you off the train…” The professor spread his hands. “Some freshmen have been rather surprised before, but a reaction like yours is unprecedented. Are you… that afraid of dragons? Fundamentally, they’re only a powerful species.”
“No!” Lu Mingfei stared into his eyes. “I’m not afraid of dragons… Have you seen The Terminator?”
“Yes. Arnold Schwarzenegger. I’m very fond of him. The current governor of California.” The professor nodded.

“Remember the scene where John Connor’s mother is at a police station? She tells the police she saw a robot that traveled back through time from an era when humanity’s nearly extinct, firing a laser rifle everywhere…” Lu Mingfei said. “And the police tell her she’s mentally ill!”
“You think I’m mentally ill?”
“Either you are or I am!” he shouted.
“All right. Some freshmen need physical evidence!” The professor clapped his hands.

The study door opened. A middle-aged man whose face practically announced I AM JAPANESE strode in with a sturdy, silver-edged black briefcase in each hand. Setting them on the desk, he bowed respectfully to Lu Mingfei and introduced himself in fluent Chinese. “I’m Masashi Toyama, a psychological counselor here at Cassell. It’s a great pleasure to meet our S-rank freshman. We haven’t had an S-rank freshman in more than forty years.”
“Really? May I ask what sort of person the one forty years ago was? An unrivaled master dragon slayer?” Lu Mingfei tried to think along their lines.
“He had the chance. But in the second semester of his sophomore year, he shot himself. So that was that,” Masashi Toyama said with complete candor.
